title: Principles
author: Ray Dalio
summary: Ray Dalio lays out the rules he developed for decision-making in life and at Bridgewater, the investment firm he founded. The core ideas are radical open-mindedness, radical transparency, and learning from mistakes.
highlights: Maturity is the ability to reject good alternatives in order to pursue even better ones.
Pain + Reflection = Progress.
Every time you confront something painful, you are at a potentially important juncture in your life-you have the opportunity to choose healthy and painful truth or unhealthy but comfortable delusion.

title: Meditations
author: Marcus Aurelius
summary: The private notebook of a Roman emperor, written as reminders to himself. He returns again and again to controlling his own judgments, accepting what he can't change, and treating other people well.
highlights: The impediment to action advances action. What stands in the way becomes the way.
It never ceases to amaze me: we all love ourselves more than other people, but care more about their opinion than our own.
Perfection of character: to live your last day, every day, without frenzy, or sloth, or pretense.

title: The Laws of Human Nature
author: Robert Greene
summary: A guide to the patterns that drive human behavior, including narcissism, envy, conformity, and short-term thinking. Greene uses historical examples to show how to recognize these traits in others and in yourself.
highlights: Human desire is never an individual phenomenon. We are social creatures and what we want almost always reflects what other people want.
You need some detachment and perspective. Get your ego to calm down. Remind yourself that winning an argument or proving your point really gets you nowhere in the long run.
Time is the greatest teacher of them all, the revealer of reality.

title: Letters From a Stoic
author: Seneca
summary: A collection of letters Seneca wrote to his friend Lucilius late in life. They give practical advice on fear, wealth, friendship, time, and death from a Stoic point of view.
highlights: We suffer more often in imagination than in reality.
It is equally faulty to trust everyone and to trust no one.
How many men, I say to myself, train their bodies, and how few train their minds!

title: 101 Essays That Will Change the Way You Think
author: Brianna Wiest
summary: A collection of short essays on emotions, habits, happiness, and self-sabotage. Most argue that how you interpret your life matters more than the circumstances themselves.
highlights: Clarity comes from doing, not thinking about doing.
Most people don’t change until not changing is the less comfortable option.
Everything is hard, but you choose your hard. You choose what’s worth it. You don’t choose whether or not you’ll suffer, but you do choose what you want to suffer for.

title: The Almanack of Naval Ravikant
author: Eric Jorgenson
summary: A compilation of Naval Ravikant's tweets, interviews, and essays, organized into two parts: building wealth and finding happiness. It covers leverage, specific knowledge, long-term thinking, and peace of mind.
highlights: Desire is a contract you make with yourself to be unhappy until you get what you want. I don’t think most of us realize that’s what it is.
Play iterated games. All the returns in life, whether in wealth, relationships, or knowledge, come from compound interest.
If you can’t see yourself working with someone for life, don’t work with them for a day.

title: The Courage to Be Disliked
author: Ichiro Kishimi & Fumitake Koga
summary: A dialogue between a philosopher and a young man that explains Alfred Adler's psychology. It argues that the past doesn't determine who you are, that most problems are about relationships, and that freedom means not living for others' approval.
highlights: We do not lack ability. We just lack courage. It all comes down to courage.
A healthy feeling of inferiority is not something that comes from comparing oneself to others; it comes from one’s comparison with one’s ideal self.
When one seeks recognition from others, and concerns oneself only with how one is judged by others, in the end, one is living other people’s lives.

title: Stillness Is the Key
author: Ryan Holiday
summary: Holiday draws on Stoic, Buddhist, and other traditions to argue that calm focus is the basis for good thinking and good work. The book is split into three parts: mind, spirit, and body.
highlights: The one thing you can’t escape in your life is yourself.
This is what the best journals look like. They aren’t for the reader. They are for the writer. To slow the mind down. To wage peace with oneself.
No one in the sway of envy or jealousy has a chance to think clearly or live peacefully.

title: Mastery
author: Robert Greene
summary: Greene studies the lives of masters such as Darwin, Faraday, and da Vinci to describe the path to excellence in a field. That path runs from finding your calling, through a long apprenticeship, to creative work.
highlights: Some people never become who they are; they stop trusting themselves; they conform to the tastes of others, and they end up wearing a mask that hides their true identity.
The moment that you rest, thinking that you have attained the level you desire, a part of your mind enters a phase of decay.
The road to mastery requires patience. You will have to keep your focus on five or ten years down the road, when you will reap the rewards of your efforts.

title: Clear Thinking
author: Shane Parrish
summary: Parrish argues that most bad decisions happen in ordinary moments, when emotion, ego, social pressure, or habit react before reasoning starts. The book covers how to spot those defaults and set up habits and conditions for better judgment.
highlights: Wisdom is turning your future hindsight into your current foresight.
Many people think they’re bad problem solvers when in fact they’re bad problem anticipators.
More dreams die from a lack of confidence than a lack of competence.

title: The 21 Irrefutable Laws of Leadership
author: John C. Maxwell
summary: Maxwell sets out 21 principles of leadership, such as influence, trust, priorities and succession. Each one comes with examples from business, sports, the military and history.
highlights: leadership cannot be awarded, appointed, or assigned. It comes only from influence, and that cannot be mandated. It must be earned. The only thing a title can buy is a little time—either to increase your level of influence with others or to undermine it.
Character makes trust possible. And trust makes leadership possible.
Followers may doubt what their leaders say, but they usually believe what they do.

title: Ego Is the Enemy
author: Ryan Holiday
summary: Holiday argues that ego, meaning an unhealthy belief in your own importance, gets in the way at every stage: when you are starting out, when you succeed and when you fail. He draws on Stoic philosophy and historical figures to make the case for humility and steady work.
highlights: What is rare is not raw talent, skill, or even confidence, but humility, diligence, and self-awareness.
Ego needs honors in order to be validated. Confidence, on the other hand, is able to wait and focus on the task at hand regardless of external recognition.
It takes a special kind of humility to grasp that you know less, even as you know and grasp more and more.

title: Lessons From an American Stoic
author: Mark Matousek
summary: Matousek presents Ralph Waldo Emerson's ideas as practical guidance. He organizes them into lessons on originality, perspective, nonconformity, resilience, courage and love, and ties them to Stoic thought.
highlights: Seeing your narrative come apart before your eyes proves how arbitrary your personal fictions are.
We underestimate the impact of confidence on our ability to flourish.
Self-reliance depends on the ability to say no without apology or explanation.

title: The Speed of Trust
author: Stephen M.R. Covey
summary: Covey argues that trust is a measurable factor in business: when trust is high, work moves faster and costs less. He breaks credibility into integrity, intent, capabilities and results, and lists behaviors that build or restore trust.
highlights: when trust is low, speed goes down and cost goes up. When trust is high, speed goes up and cost goes down.
Ultimately micromanagers who trust only themselves can take their companies only as far as they themselves can take them.
What creates trust, in the end, is the leader’s manifest respect for the followers. —JAMES O’TOOLE, AUTHOR OF LEADING CHANGE

title: Aristotle's Way
author: Edith Hall
summary: Hall, a classicist, explains Aristotle's ethics as a practical guide to a happy life. The book covers finding your potential, making decisions, communicating, building character, friendship and facing death.
highlights: Aristotle believed that if you train yourself to be good, by working on your virtues and controlling your vices, you will discover that a happy state of mind comes from habitually doing the right thing.
The trick is to find out what you like doing and have an aptitude for, and then stick at it.
Time spent worrying about things which you cannot change is wasted.

title: The 9 Types of Leadership
author: Beatrice Chestnut
summary: Chestnut uses the Enneagram to describe nine personality types and how each one tends to lead. She argues that good leadership depends on noticing your own habitual, defensive patterns and working past them.
highlights: Most of all, leaders (and all of us) need effective ways to learn to be kinder and more compassionate with ourselves and with others, and less defensive, reactive, and inflexible in the ways we respond to the people and events around us.

the ability to achieve and maintain harmonious and productive working relationships depends on one thing: how well the people involved have the humility and the will to understand and manage themselves and understand and relate well to others.
other people don’t all view the world the way we do; different people can look at the same situation and see completely different things.

title: The 33 Strategies of War
author: Robert Greene
summary: Greene takes 33 strategies from military history and applies them to conflict in everyday life and work. They cover defense, offense, unconventional tactics and self-command.
highlights: Getting along with other people is an important skill to have, but it comes with a danger: by always seeking the path of least resistance, the path of conciliation, you forget who you are, and you sink into the center with everyone else.
Unintimidate yourself. Intimidation will always threaten your presence of mind.
Once you learn patience, your options suddenly expand.

title: The Courage to Be Happy
author: Ichiro Kishimi & Fumitake Koga
summary: This sequel to The Courage to Be Disliked is a dialogue between a philosopher and a young teacher about Alfred Adler's psychology. It covers praise and punishment, self-reliance, work, friendship and love.
highlights: The past does not decide now. It is your now that decides the past.
Instead of seeking approval, one has to approve oneself, with one’s own mind.
a person’s worth is not something that is decided by what kind of work they engage in. It is decided by the attitude with which they undertake that work.

title: Heroic Leadership
author: Chris Lowney
summary: Lowney, a former Jesuit seminarian who became a banker, looks at how the Jesuits built a lasting global organization. He identifies four principles behind it: self-awareness, ingenuity, love and heroism.
highlights: Only those who know their weaknesses can deal with them or even hope to conquer them.
Heroic leaders don’t bide their time until the big moment comes along; they grasp the opportunities within reach and extract as much richness from them as possible.
Companies aren’t self-aware; people are. And organizations don’t love; only humans do. Leadership is a personal choice.

title: The Effective Executive
author: Peter F. Drucker
summary: Drucker describes the habits that make knowledge workers and managers effective: knowing where their time goes, focusing on contribution, building on strengths, doing first things first and making sound decisions.
highlights: People in general, and knowledge workers in particular, grow according to the demands they make on themselves.
Strong people always have strong weaknesses too.
a decision that has to satisfy two different and at bottom incompatible specifications is not a decision but a prayer for a miracle

title: Scaling People
author: Claire Hughes Johnson
summary: A manager's handbook from Stripe's former COO on building a company's operating system as it grows: planning, hiring, team development, feedback, and communication. It pairs frameworks with templates and exercises for leaders at growing companies.
highlights: I often think of my work as a manager as clearing the path my team will need to travel. Anything that slows them down is on me.

Good communication is about providing timely and honest information, including being willing to acknowledge mistakes. People forgive mistakes, but they lose trust when information is hidden, false, or misleading, or when leadership says something but doesn’t follow through.

Every part of the stack—the team, the division, and the company—should have a mission. A team’s mission should ladder up to the division’s mission, and the division’s mission should ladder up to the company’s mission.

title: Working Backwards
author: Colin Bryar & Bill Carr
summary: Two longtime Amazon executives describe the company's management practices, including single-threaded leadership, six-page narratives, the PR/FAQ process, Bar Raiser hiring, and input metrics. They show how those practices shaped Kindle, Prime, Prime Video, and AWS.
highlights: “The best way to fail at inventing something is by making it somebody’s part-time job.”
There’s a saying often heard at Amazon: “Good intentions don’t work. Mechanisms do.”
Input metrics measure things that, done right, bring about the desired results in your output metrics.

title: Play Bigger
author: Al Ramadan, Dave Peterson, Christopher Lochhead & Kevin Maney
summary: The authors argue that the most valuable companies create and define new market categories rather than compete in existing ones. The book lays out "category design": framing the problem, writing a point of view, and designing product, company, and category together.
highlights: A company that best frames a problem is the company that often comes to define and take the category. Put another way: winning companies today market the problem, not just the solution.
Customers will ask for better. You want to hear different. Look for what’s missing, not what can be improved.

The taxonomy becomes “truth” and it describes all the elements of the solution and how they fit into the category. Words matter. Category kings lead with language. The name of products and features can change the way people value them.

title: Four Thousand Weeks
author: Oliver Burkeman
summary: A book about time management that starts from the fact that the average life lasts about four thousand weeks. Burkeman argues that trying to get everything done makes things worse, and that accepting limits and making hard choices leads to a better use of time.
highlights: Productivity is a trap. Becoming more efficient just makes you more rushed, and trying to clear the decks simply makes them fill up again faster.
The real measure of any time management technique is whether or not it helps you neglect the right things.
We’re all in the position of medieval stonemasons, adding a few more bricks to a cathedral whose completion we know we’ll never see. The cathedral’s still worth building, all the same.

title: On Writing Well
author: William Zinsser
summary: A guide to writing nonfiction, covering clarity, simplicity, cutting clutter, rewriting, and writing in your own voice. Later chapters apply those principles to interviews, travel, memoir, science, business, and criticism.
highlights: If you find that writing is hard, it’s because it is hard.
Readers want the person who is talking to them to sound genuine. Therefore a fundamental rule is: be yourself.
Readers should always feel that you know more about your subject than you’ve put in writing.

title: The Daily Stoic
author: Ryan Holiday & Stephen Hanselman
summary: A year of daily readings, each pairing a passage from Marcus Aurelius, Seneca, Epictetus, or another Stoic with a short commentary. The readings are grouped into monthly themes such as clarity, judgment, acceptance, and mortality.
highlights: Ask yourself: What haven’t I considered? Why is this thing the way it is? Am I part of the problem here or the solution? Could I be wrong here?
“Throw out your conceited opinions, for it is impossible for a person to begin to learn what he thinks he already knows.” —EPICTETUS, DISCOURSES, 2.17.1

“If a person gave away your body to some passerby, you’d be furious. Yet you hand over your mind to anyone who comes along, so they may abuse you, leaving it disturbed and troubled—have you no shame in that?” —EPICTETUS, ENCHIRIDION, 28

title: What You Do Is Who You Are
author: Ben Horowitz
summary: Horowitz argues that a company's culture is defined by what its people actually do, not by stated values. He draws on examples like the Haitian revolution, the samurai, Genghis Khan, and a prison gang leader to show how leaders shape culture through their actions.
highlights: If you aren’t yourself, even you won’t follow you.
If somebody behaves in a way you can’t believe, remember that your culture somehow made that acceptable.
The truth about telling the truth is that it doesn’t come easy. It’s not natural. What’s natural is telling people what they want to hear.

title: Dare to Lead
author: Brené Brown
summary: Brown applies her research on vulnerability, shame, and courage to leadership. She covers how leaders can build trust, give honest feedback, live by their values, and recover from setbacks.
highlights: Clear is kind. Unclear is unkind.
Integrity is choosing courage over comfort; it’s choosing what’s right over what’s fun, fast, or easy; and it’s practicing your values, not just professing them.
I know I’m ready to give feedback when I’m willing to put the problem in front of us rather than between us (or sliding it toward you).

title: A Calendar of Wisdom
author: Leo Tolstoy
summary: A collection Tolstoy compiled late in life with one reading for each day of the year. It mixes his own thoughts with sayings from philosophers, religious texts, and writers on topics like kindness, work, wealth, and self-improvement.
highlights: If you want to do a good deed, do it now. The time will pass, and you will not have the chance again.
The more urgently you want to speak, the more likely it is that you will say something foolish.

When I sit on the seashore and listen to the waves beating on the sand, I feel free from any obligation, and I think that all the people of the world can change their constitutions without me. —HENRY DAVID THOREAU

title: Fallen Leaves
author: Will Durant
summary: Short essays the historian wrote near the end of his life, published after his death. He gives his views on youth, aging, religion, war, politics, art, science, education, and death.
highlights: Life is that which is discontent, which struggles and seeks, which suffers and creates.
Let us ask the gods not for possessions, but for things to do; happiness is in making things rather than in consuming them.
Intellect is the capacity for acquiring and accumulating ideas; intelligence is the ability to use experience—even the experience of others—for the clarification and attainment of one’s ends.

title: Lighter
author: Yung Pueblo
summary: A short book on emotional healing and self-awareness, drawing on meditation practice. It covers letting go of old reactions, managing ego, and how personal change affects relationships and community.
highlights: your first reaction is your past your intentional response is your present
Ego craves to win, but loving clarity seeks to understand.
Real maturity is keeping your peace in the midst of a disagreement.

title: BE 2.0
author: Jim Collins
summary: An updated edition of Collins's 1992 guide for small and mid-sized companies that want to last. It covers leadership, getting the right people, vision and values, strategy, and day-to-day execution.
highlights: How do you know if you have a truly great business? Warren Buffett has the best answer: You don’t have to hold a prayer meeting to raise prices.
Innovation often comes from seeing the relationship between unconnected ideas and melding them together.
The first step in being built to last is don’t die. The only mistakes you can learn from are the ones you survive.

title: What They Forgot to Teach You at School
author: The School of Life
summary: A collection of short essays on the emotional skills school leaves out. Topics include self-compassion, kindness, repairing relationships, managing moods, and living with anxiety.
highlights: Hating ourselves is the easy bit. Learning to give ourselves a break is the true, rare and properly adult achievement.
Small acts of kindness are a way of lending others small change in the currency of hope and courage which we depend on for our emotional survival.
It can feel so much easier to get offended with someone than to dare to imagine they might have something important to tell us.

title: Antifragile
author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb
summary: Taleb argues that some things gain from volatility, stress, and disorder, and calls them antifragile. He applies the idea to health, economics, innovation, and ethics, and argues for limiting downside while leaving room for upside.
highlights: Antifragility is beyond resilience or robustness. The resilient resists shocks and stays the same; the antifragile gets better.
Steve Jobs figured out that “you have to work hard to get your thinking clean to make it simple.”
My idea of the modern Stoic sage is someone who transforms fear into prudence, pain into information, mistakes into initiation, and desire into undertaking.

title: The Bhagavad Gita
author: Eknath Easwaran (translator)
summary: A Hindu scripture in which Krishna advises the warrior Arjuna before a battle. Easwaran's translation and introductions explain its teachings on duty, selfless action, detachment from results, and meditation.
highlights: Since the Self is the core of every personality, no one needs to acquire goodness or compassion; they are already there. All that is necessary is to remove the selfish habits that hide them.
When meditation is mastered, the mind is unwavering like the flame of a lamp in a windless place.
Give freely. Be self-controlled, sincere, truthful, loving, and full of the desire to serve.

title: Truman
author: David McCullough
summary: A biography of Harry S. Truman, from his Missouri farm upbringing through the Senate and his presidency. It covers the end of World War II, the Marshall Plan, and the early Cold War.
highlights: Always be nice to the people who can’t talk back to you.
More than once in his presidency, Truman would be remembered saying it was remarkable how much could be accomplished if you didn’t care who received the credit.
Truman remarked, “You never know what’s in you until you have to do it.”

title: Zero to One
author: Peter Thiel
summary: Thiel's notes on startups, built around the idea that real progress comes from creating new things, not copying existing ones. He argues that great companies escape competition, build monopolies, and rest on a secret others have missed.
highlights: What important truth do very few people agree with you on?
The most contrarian thing of all is not to oppose the crowd but to think for yourself.
All happy companies are different: each one earns a monopoly by solving a unique problem. All failed companies are the same: they failed to escape competition.

title: As a Man Thinketh
author: James Allen
summary: A short 1903 essay arguing that a person's character and circumstances come from their habitual thoughts. Allen says that changing how you think is the way to change your life.
highlights: Men do not attract that which they want, but that which they are.
Men are anxious to improve their circumstances, but are unwilling to improve themselves; they therefore remain bound.
We imagine that thought can be kept secret, but it cannot; it rapidly crystallizes into habit, and habit solidifies into circumstance.

title: It Doesn't Have to Be Crazy at Work
author: Jason Fried & David Heinemeier Hansson
summary: The founders of Basecamp describe how they run a calm company. They cover 40-hour weeks, protecting time and attention, writing instead of meeting, and avoiding growth at all costs.
highlights: A fractured hour isn’t really an hour—it’s a mess of minutes.
Don’t meet, write. Don’t react, consider.
Calm requires getting comfortable with enough.

title: From Strength to Strength
author: Arthur C. Brooks
summary: Brooks looks at professional decline in middle age and how to handle it. He suggests shifting from raw problem-solving to wisdom and teaching, letting go of success addiction, and investing in relationships.
highlights: Satisfaction comes not from chasing bigger and bigger things, but paying attention to smaller and smaller things.
Success, the fruit of excellence, becomes an addiction. All because of pride.
Being open to reevaluating our ideas about ourselves can keep us from getting stuck in patterns that aren’t true to our changing selves.
